hints: Focus on what type of compound propanone is and what type of reagent NaBH4 is.
Propanone is a ketone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, and NaBH4 is a reducing agent that adds hydrogen across the C=O bond.
Think about where the OH ends up when you reduce a ketone with the carbonyl carbon in the middle of the chain.
walkthrough:
**Identify the starting material**

Propanone is the simplest ketone. Its structure has the carbonyl group in the middle of a 3-carbon chain.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$$

**Recall what NaBH4 does**

Sodium borohydride, $\text{NaBH}_4$, is a mild reducing agent. It reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. It does not reduce all the way to an alkane.

$$\text{C=O} + 2[H] \rightarrow \text{CH-OH}$$

**Apply to propanone**

Reduction adds H to the carbonyl carbon and H to the oxygen to make an OH group. Because the C=O carbon is carbon-2, the OH stays on carbon-2.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 2[H] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$$
This product is propan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol.

options.A: Correct. Reduction of the ketone propanone gives the secondary alcohol with the OH on carbon-2, which is propan-2-ol.
options.B: Incorrect. Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol with OH on carbon-1. It would come from reducing propanal, not from reducing propanone. The carbonyl position does not move during reduction.
options.C: Incorrect. Propanal is an aldehyde. NaBH4 is a reducing agent, not an oxidising agent, and it cannot convert a ketone into an aldehyde. This confuses reduction with a different functional group interconversion.
options.D: Incorrect. Propane is an alkane with no oxygen. NaBH4 is too mild to remove oxygen completely. Complete reduction to an alkane would need much stronger conditions, not NaBH4.
